title: Muhammad, the Qur'an and the First Community
bigQuestion: How did one man's message in a mountain cave become the faith of a whole community?

story.title: The Trustworthy One on the Mountain
story.kicker: A respected merchant of Mecca goes to a quiet cave to think, and Muslims say his life changed there.
paragraphs: Mecca, around the year 610. The city sits in a dry valley in western Arabia. Camel caravans come and go, carrying spices, cloth and leather. Traders from many tribes crowd its markets. At the center of the city stands the Kaaba, a cube-shaped building that Arabs from far away visit.

Among the merchants is a man of about forty named Muhammad. He lost his parents as a child and was raised by his grandfather and then his uncle. He works in the caravan trade. People in Mecca call him al-Amin, which means "the trustworthy." They leave their valuables with him because they know he is honest.

Muhammad often climbs a rocky mountain outside the city. Near the top is a small cave called Hira. There he spends nights alone, thinking and praying. According to Muslim tradition, one night in the month of Ramadan, the angel Gabriel (Jibril in Arabic) came to him in the cave.

Muslims tell that the angel gave one command: "Recite!" Muhammad answered that he was not a reciter. The command came again, and then the first words of what Muslims call the Qur'an. Shaken, Muhammad hurried home to his wife, Khadijah. She comforted him and, in Muslim tradition, became the first person to accept his message.

Over the next twenty-some years, Muslims believe, more revelations came. They were memorized, recited and later gathered into one book. Today about two billion people call themselves Muslims. This chapter follows the story as Muslims tell it and as historians study it.
story.think: Why do you think people in Mecca trusted Muhammad before he ever began to preach? Why might that matter to the story Muslims tell?

lessons.title: Arabia Before Islam
lessons.mainIdea: Before Islam, Arabia was a land of trading towns and desert tribes, with Mecca and its Kaaba at the center of trade and worship.
reading: Picture the Arabian Peninsula around 600 CE. Most of it is desert. People live in oasis towns or move with herds of camels and goats. They belong to *tribes*, large family groups that protect their members. Loyalty to the tribe mattered more than loyalty to any king, because Arabia had no single ruler.

Mecca was a trading town. Caravans carried goods between Yemen in the south and Syria in the north. The powerful Quraysh tribe ran much of this trade. Mecca also held the *Kaaba*, a stone shrine. Each year, people from many tribes came to worship there, and fighting was forbidden during certain months so pilgrims and traders could travel safely.

Most Arabs at this time worshipped many gods. In Muslim tradition, the Kaaba held hundreds of idols, or statues of gods. Some Arabs were Jews or Christians, and a few, called hanifs in Muslim sources, worshipped one God. Muslims call this time the Jahiliyya, meaning "the age of ignorance," because in their view it came before God's final message.

words.d: a large group of families who share an ancestor and protect one another
a cube-shaped shrine in Mecca; Muslims believe Abraham and his son Ishmael built it to worship one God
the leading tribe of Mecca, which Muhammad was born into

look.title: A Market Town and a Shrine
look.text: Mecca had little water and poor soil for farming. Yet it grew rich. Caravans stopped there on the road between Yemen and Syria. Pilgrims came to the Kaaba each year, and during the sacred months, tribes agreed not to fight.
look.prompt: How could a shrine and a trade route help each other? Give one way the pilgrims helped the merchants.

check.q: What was the Kaaba in Mecca before Islam?
choices: A shrine that people from many tribes visited
A royal palace for the king of Arabia
A school for studying the Qur'an
A Christian church built by the Romans
check.why: The Kaaba was a shrine at the center of Mecca, visited by people from many tribes.

check.q: Why did tribes matter so much in Arabia around 600 CE?
choices: The Roman emperor chose tribal leaders
There was no single ruler, so the tribe protected its members
Tribes were religious groups that each had one holy book
check.why: Arabia had no king over everyone, so a person's tribe gave protection.

check.q: What does the Arabic term Jahiliyya mean, as Muslims use it?
choices: The age of ignorance before Islam
check.why: Muslims use Jahiliyya, "the age of ignorance," for the time before the Qur'an's message.

lessons.title: The Cave and the Message
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims believe that around 610 CE, the angel Gabriel brought Muhammad the first words of the Qur'an in the cave of Hira.
reading: Muhammad was born in Mecca around 570 CE. He grew up as an orphan and became a trader. At about age twenty-five he married Khadijah, a widow who ran her own caravan business. As an adult, he often went to the cave of Hira to be alone and reflect.

Muslims believe that around 610 CE, the angel Gabriel came to him there with a message from God. They call these messages *revelation*, words that God makes known. The first words, in Muslim tradition, are the opening of Surah 96: a command to recite in the name of the Lord who created.

For Muslims, this night made Muhammad a *prophet*, a person God chooses to carry a message. The Qur'an describes him as the "seal of the prophets," the last in a line that Muslims say includes Abraham, Moses and Jesus. Jews and Christians have their own teachings about those figures and do not share this view of Muhammad.

words.d: a message that believers say God makes known to people
a person who, believers say, is chosen by God to deliver God's message
the mountain cave near Mecca where Muslims say the first revelation came

look.title: The First Words
look.text: Recite in the name of your Lord, who created. He created the human being from a clinging clot. Recite, for your Lord is most generous, who taught by the pen, taught people what they did not know.
look.cite: Qur'an, Surah 96 (al-Alaq), verses 1–5; paraphrased in plain English
look.prompt: The first words Muslims say were revealed are about reciting and the pen. What do they suggest about how Muslims value learning?

check.q: About when do Muslims date the first revelation to Muhammad?
check.why: Muslim tradition places the first revelation around 610 CE, when Muhammad was about forty.

check.q: Who was Khadijah?
choices: Muhammad's wife, who in Muslim tradition first accepted his message
The angel who brought the revelation
A queen of Yemen who attacked Mecca
check.why: Khadijah was Muhammad's wife; Muslims honor her as the first believer.

check.q: What does the Qur'an mean by calling Muhammad the "seal of the prophets"?
choices: Muslims believe he is the last prophet
He was the first prophet ever
check.why: Muslims read "seal of the prophets" to mean Muhammad is the final prophet.

lessons.title: From Mecca to Medina
lessons.mainIdea: In 622 Muhammad and his followers moved from Mecca to Medina, a journey called the hijra that starts the Islamic calendar.
reading: Muhammad began to preach in Mecca. He taught that there is one God, that people will be judged for their deeds, and that the rich must care for the poor. Some people joined him. Many leaders of the Quraysh did not. His message challenged the gods of the Kaaba and the trade that pilgrims brought.

The early Muslims faced insults, boycotts and violence. In 622, people from the town of Yathrib invited Muhammad to lead them. He and his followers moved there. This move is called the *hijra*, Arabic for "migration." Yathrib became known as Medina, "the city" of the Prophet.

In Medina, Muslims formed their first *umma*, or community. Muhammad was both its religious teacher and its leader. Medina also had Jewish tribes, and an agreement often called the Constitution of Medina set out rules for the town's groups. Muslims later made 622 the first year of their calendar.

words.d: the migration of Muhammad and his followers from Mecca to Medina in 622
the community of all Muslims
the city north of Mecca, once called Yathrib, where Muhammad led the first Muslim community

look.title: Why Start a Calendar Here?
look.text: Muslims could have started their calendar with Muhammad's birth or with the first revelation. Instead they chose the hijra in 622. That was the year the believers first lived together as a community with their own leader and rules.
look.prompt: Why might a community choose its move to Medina, not a birthday, as year one? What does the choice show about what Muslims value?

check.q: What was the hijra?
choices: The move from Mecca to Medina in 622
check.why: The hijra is the migration to Medina in 622.

check.q: Why did many Quraysh leaders oppose Muhammad's preaching?
choices: He asked them to move to Egypt
His message of one God challenged the gods of the Kaaba and the trade around it
He wanted to become king of Rome
He banned all trade in Mecca
check.why: Teaching one God questioned the Kaaba's idols, which drew pilgrims and trade.

check.q: Which event marks year one of the Islamic calendar?
check.why: The Islamic calendar counts its years from the hijra of 622.

lessons.title: Return to Mecca
lessons.mainIdea: In 630 Muhammad returned to Mecca, and Muslims rededicated the Kaaba to one God; he died in Medina in 632.
reading: For several years, Medina and Mecca were at war. Battles such as Badr (624) and Uhud (625) are well known in Muslim history. In 628 the two sides signed a truce at a place called Hudaybiyya. When the truce broke down, Muhammad marched toward Mecca with a large army in 630.

Mecca surrendered with little fighting. Muslim sources say Muhammad forgave most of his old enemies. He had the idols removed from the Kaaba. Muslims believe this returned the shrine to the worship of one God, as they say Abraham first intended. Many Arab tribes then joined the Muslim community.

In 632 Muhammad made a pilgrimage to Mecca and gave what Muslims call the *Farewell Sermon*. He died later that year in Medina. His followers faced a hard question: who should lead the community now? Their answers to that question still shape Islam today.

words.d: an agreement to stop fighting for a time
the speech Muslims say Muhammad gave at his last pilgrimage in 632

look.title: Key Years in Muhammad's Life
look.cite: Common dates from Muslim tradition and historians; early dates are approximate
look.prompt: How many years passed between the first revelation and Muhammad's death? How many of those years did he spend in Medina?

check.q: What did Muhammad do at the Kaaba after returning to Mecca in 630?
choices: He gave it to the Byzantine emperor
check.why: Muslim sources say he removed the idols and dedicated the Kaaba to one God.

check.q: In what year did Muhammad die?
check.why: Muhammad died in Medina in 632, after his final pilgrimage.

check.q: What big question did Muslims face after Muhammad's death?
choices: Whether to keep fasting in Ramadan
Whether to move back to Yathrib
check.why: Muhammad's death raised the question of leadership, which later divided Sunni and Shia.

lessons.title: A Book Meant to Be Recited
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims believe the Qur'an is God's word in Arabic, first memorized and recited, then gathered into one written book.
reading: The word *Qur'an* means "recitation." Muslims believe it is the exact word of God, given to Muhammad through Gabriel over about 23 years. At first, followers memorized the verses and wrote some on bone, leather and palm leaves. Reciting aloud was the main way people learned it.

Muslim tradition says the verses were collected into one book soon after Muhammad died. Under the third caliph, Uthman (ruled 644–656), a standard copy was made and sent to major cities. Muslims hold that the text has been kept the same since then.

Muslims believe the Qur'an is fully the Qur'an only in Arabic. Translations help readers understand the meaning, but most Muslims treat them as explanations, not as the Qur'an itself. Many Muslims around the world pray in Arabic even when it is not their home language. A person who memorizes the whole book is honored with the title *hafiz*.

words.d: the holy book of Islam; the word means "recitation"
a person who has memorized the whole Qur'an
a successor who led the Muslim community after Muhammad

look.title: A Class of Young Reciters
look.text: On a Saturday morning at a mosque in the Chicago suburbs, a group of children sits on the carpet. A teacher recites a short surah in Arabic. The children repeat it line by line. Some of them speak English at home, some Urdu, some Arabic. All of them learn the same words.
look.prompt: Why might a community teach children to recite the Qur'an in Arabic, even if they speak another language at home?

check.q: What does the word Qur'an mean?
check.why: Qur'an means "recitation," because Muslims first learned it by reciting aloud.

check.q: How do most Muslims view an English translation of the Qur'an?
choices: As an explanation of the meaning, not the Qur'an itself
check.why: Muslims believe the Qur'an is fully itself only in Arabic; translations explain its meaning.

check.q: What is a hafiz?
choices: A person who has memorized the whole Qur'an
A tax paid to the poor
check.why: A hafiz has memorized the entire Qur'an.

lessons.title: Surahs, Ayahs and the Sunnah
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an has 114 surahs made of ayahs, and Muslims also learn from the Sunnah, the example of Muhammad recorded in hadith.
reading: The Qur'an is divided into 114 chapters called *surahs*. Each surah is made of verses called *ayahs*. After the short opening surah, the surahs are arranged roughly from longest to shortest. So the Qur'an does not tell one story from start to end, the way a history book might.

The first surah, al-Fatiha ("The Opening"), is only seven verses long. Muslims recite it in every unit of daily prayer. It praises God as merciful and asks to be guided on the straight path. Short surahs near the end, such as Surah 112, are often the first ones children learn.

Muslims also learn from the *Sunnah*, the example of how Muhammad lived. Reports of his words and actions are called *hadith*. Scholars sorted hadith by how reliable their chains of reporters seemed. Sunni and Shia Muslims use partly different hadith collections.

words.d: a chapter of the Qur'an; there are 114
a verse of the Qur'an; the word also means "sign"
the example of Muhammad's life, which Muslims try to follow
a report of something Muhammad said or did

look.title: A Short Surah on One God
look.text: Say: He is God, the One. God, the Eternal, on whom all depend. He does not give birth, and He was not born. And there is none like Him.
look.cite: Qur'an, Surah 112 (al-Ikhlas), verses 1–4; paraphrased in plain English
look.prompt: This surah has only four verses. What does it say God is like, and what does it say God is not like?

check.q: How many surahs are in the Qur'an?
check.why: The Qur'an has 114 surahs.

check.q: How are most surahs of the Qur'an arranged?
choices: In the order of Muhammad's life
check.why: After al-Fatiha, surahs run roughly from longest to shortest.

check.q: What is a hadith?
choices: A report of Muhammad's words or actions
check.why: Hadith are reports of what Muhammad said or did; together they show the Sunnah.

lessons.title: Faith and Prayer
lessons.mainIdea: The first two pillars are the shahada, the statement of faith, and salat, prayer five times a day.
reading: Muslims describe five core practices as the *Five Pillars* of Islam. Like pillars holding up a building, they support a Muslim's life. They appear in a well-known hadith. Sunni and Shia Muslims both keep these practices, though Shia teachers list their core duties a little differently.

The first pillar is the *shahada*, the statement of faith: "There is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God." Saying it sincerely, Muslims believe, is how a person enters Islam. Muslims repeat it in prayer and whisper it to newborn babies.

The second pillar is *salat*, prayer five times a day: at dawn, midday, afternoon, sunset and night. Before praying, Muslims wash in a set way. They face the Kaaba in Mecca, a direction called the qibla. Prayer includes standing, bowing and touching the forehead to the ground.

words.d: five core practices of Islam: shahada, salat, zakat, sawm and hajj
the Muslim statement of faith in one God and in Muhammad as God's messenger
the prayer Muslims perform five times a day
the direction of the Kaaba in Mecca, which Muslims face in prayer

look.title: A Prayer Rug at Lunchtime
look.text: A nurse in a Chicago hospital has a short break at midday. She checks an app that shows the qibla, which from Chicago points roughly northeast. She washes her face, hands and feet, lays down a small rug in a quiet room, and prays for about five minutes before going back to work.
look.prompt: Which parts of salat can you find in this scene? What might a workplace do to make this easier?

check.q: How many times a day do Muslims perform salat?
check.why: Salat is performed five times a day, from dawn to night.

check.q: What is the qibla?
choices: The direction of the Kaaba that Muslims face in prayer
check.why: The qibla is the direction toward the Kaaba in Mecca.

check.q: Which pillar is the statement "There is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God"?
check.why: The shahada is the Muslim statement of faith.

lessons.title: Giving and Fasting
lessons.mainIdea: Zakat is giving part of one's wealth to people in need, and sawm is fasting from dawn to sunset in the month of Ramadan.
reading: The third pillar is *zakat*, giving to those in need. Muslims who have savings above a set amount give a share each year, commonly 2.5 percent. The Qur'an lists who should receive it, including the poor. Muslims believe zakat purifies wealth and reminds them that it comes from God. Many also give extra charity, called sadaqa.

The fourth pillar is *sawm*, fasting during *Ramadan*, the ninth month of the Islamic year. From dawn until sunset, adult Muslims who are able do not eat or drink. Children, the sick, travelers and some others are excused. Many families wake before dawn for a meal and break the fast at sunset.

Muslims believe the Qur'an was first revealed in Ramadan. So many try to read or hear the whole Qur'an during the month, often at special night prayers. The month ends with Eid al-Fitr, the Festival of Breaking the Fast, with prayers, new clothes, gifts and meals.

words.d: required yearly giving of part of one's wealth to people in need
fasting; in Islam, not eating or drinking from dawn to sunset in Ramadan
the ninth month of the Islamic calendar, the month of fasting
the festival that ends Ramadan

look.title: Why Fast?
look.text: You who believe, fasting is prescribed for you, as it was prescribed for those before you, so that you may become mindful of God.
look.cite: Qur'an, Surah 2 (al-Baqarah), verse 183; paraphrased in plain English
look.prompt: According to this verse, what is the purpose of fasting? Who else does the verse say was asked to fast?

check.q: What share of savings do Muslims commonly give each year as zakat?
check.why: Zakat is commonly figured as 2.5 percent of savings above a set amount.

check.q: Which Muslims are excused from the Ramadan fast?
choices: Children, the sick and travelers, among others
People who pray five times a day
check.why: Children, the sick, travelers and some others are excused from sawm.

check.q: Which festival marks the end of Ramadan?
check.why: Eid al-Fitr, the Festival of Breaking the Fast, ends Ramadan.

lessons.title: The Pilgrimage to Mecca
lessons.mainIdea: The hajj is a pilgrimage to Mecca that Muslims who are able should make once in a lifetime.
reading: The fifth pillar is the *hajj*, the pilgrimage to Mecca. It takes place each year in Dhul Hijjah, the last month of the Islamic calendar. Every adult Muslim who is healthy and can afford it is expected to go at least once. In recent years, about two million people have made the hajj at once.

Pilgrims put on simple white clothing called *ihram*. For men it is two unsewn white cloths. Muslims say this shows that everyone is equal before God, rich or poor. Pilgrims walk seven times around the Kaaba and walk between two small hills, remembering Hagar searching for water for her son Ishmael.

Pilgrims also stand in prayer on the plain of Arafat. Then Muslims everywhere celebrate Eid al-Adha, the Festival of the Sacrifice. It remembers the story of Abraham's willingness to sacrifice his son, which appears in the Qur'an. Families share meat with relatives and with the poor.

words.d: the pilgrimage to Mecca that Muslims who are able make once in a lifetime
the simple white clothing and holy state of a pilgrim on hajj
the Festival of the Sacrifice, held during the hajj season

look.title: Two Million in White
look.text: A letter home from the hajj, 1964: an American pilgrim writes that he saw people of every color eating from the same plate and praying side by side. That pilgrim was Malcolm X. He said the experience changed how he thought about race.
look.prompt: Why might the plain white clothing of ihram make pilgrims feel equal? How did the hajj affect Malcolm X, according to his letter?

check.q: Why do pilgrims on hajj wear simple white clothing?
choices: To show that all are equal before God
Because white is the color of Ramadan
To show which tribe they belong to
Because it is the uniform of the caliph
check.why: Muslims say ihram shows equality before God, since rich and poor dress alike.

check.q: Whom do pilgrims remember when they walk between two small hills?
choices: Hagar, searching for water for Ishmael
check.why: Walking between the hills recalls Hagar's search for water for her son Ishmael.

check.q: Which statement about the hajj is correct?
choices: Every Muslim must go every year
It is made in the month of Ramadan
Muslims who are able should go at least once
check.why: The hajj is required once in a lifetime for Muslims who are healthy and can afford it.

lessons.title: Sunni and Shia
lessons.mainIdea: Sunni and Shia Muslims share the Qur'an and the Five Pillars but disagree about who should have led after Muhammad.
reading: After Muhammad died in 632, most of his companions chose Abu Bakr, his close friend, as the first *caliph*. Those who accepted this line of leaders became known as *Sunni* Muslims, from sunnah, "the way." Today most Muslims, about 85 to 90 percent, are Sunni.

Another group believed Muhammad had chosen his cousin and son-in-law, Ali, to lead. They became the *Shia*, from shiat Ali, "the party of Ali." Shia Muslims honor a line of leaders called imams, starting with Ali. Most Shia live in Iran, Iraq, Bahrain, Azerbaijan and Lebanon, with many elsewhere.

In 680, Ali's son Husayn was killed with his small band at Karbala, in Iraq. Shia Muslims mourn him each year on Ashura, the tenth day of the month of Muharram. Sunni and Shia Muslims pray, fast and make the hajj. Many Muslims stress what the two groups share.

words.d: the larger branch of Islam, which accepted the first caliphs chosen by Muhammad's companions
the branch of Islam that holds Ali and his descendants should have led after Muhammad
a prayer leader; for Shia Muslims, also one of the chosen leaders descended from Ali
the tenth of Muharram; Shia Muslims mourn Husayn's death at Karbala on this day

check.q: What was the first disagreement between Sunni and Shia Muslims about?
choices: Who should lead the community after Muhammad
How many surahs are in the Qur'an
check.why: The split began over leadership after Muhammad's death.

check.q: Whom do Shia Muslims believe should have been the first leader after Muhammad?

check.q: What do Shia Muslims remember on Ashura?

check.why: On Ashura, Shia Muslims mourn Husayn, killed at Karbala in 680.

lessons.title: The Mosque and the Moon
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims gather at the mosque, especially for Friday prayer, and follow a lunar calendar whose months move through the seasons.
reading: A *mosque* is a place where Muslims pray together. The Arabic word masjid means "place of bowing down." Inside there are no statues or pictures of people. A niche in the wall, the mihrab, shows the qibla. Many mosques have a tall tower called a minaret, from which the call to prayer is given.

At midday on Friday, Muslims gather for jumu'ah, the congregational prayer. A leader gives a short sermon, then leads the prayer. Men are expected to attend. Women may attend and often pray in their own section. Mosques also hold classes, weddings, meals and community events.

The *Islamic calendar* follows the moon. Each month begins with the new crescent moon, so the year has about 354 days. That is about 11 days shorter than the solar year. So Ramadan comes about 11 days earlier each year and moves through every season over about 33 years.

words.d: a Muslim place of prayer; in Arabic, masjid
a tall tower of a mosque, from which the call to prayer is given
the Friday midday prayer that Muslims pray together
a calendar of 12 moon-based months that counts years from the hijra

look.title: Moon Year and Sun Year

look.cite: Standard calendar facts; the lunar year has 354 or 355 days
look.prompt: If Ramadan begins in March one year, about when will it begin three years later?

check.q: When do Muslims gather for their weekly congregational prayer?

check.q: Why does Ramadan come at a different time each year on the everyday calendar?
choices: The Islamic calendar follows the moon and is about 11 days shorter

check.why: The lunar year is about 354 days, so Ramadan shifts about 11 days earlier each solar year.
